doc.title: Tyner McCoy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Conga lessons, dance and Philadelphia's culture
summary: Aisha and Tyner recall conga teachers, the mother's shop as the rehearsal place, dance schools and Philly's rich cultural life.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Also he took conga lessons, he played congas.
Really? So you were taking conga lessons.
Yeah, I had to stop that though because what happens when you hit the rim . . . (of the drum) it hurts, so I had to stop that, but I did play congas.
And who were you studying with?
What do you mean? Congas?
Studying congas, you were just picking it up?
Garvin Masseaux.
Oh that’s right, Garvin Masseaux.
Saka Acquaye. Philly had a lot of things with dance, congas, and drums, a lot of culture in Philly. We grew up with a lot of culture.
What centers, were there community centers, where was this music being performed and rehearsed? Was there a community center? Where did it germinate?
In my mother’s shop. We didn’t have a hall.
Bobby Crowder (had his own place) . . .
Bobby Crowder, the drummer?
Yeah.
Yes! He knew my sister, you know Bobby Crowder, conga player? Yes, Garvin Masseaux, yup. All them, they were all together.
So that was your musical fraternity.
And then my hero moved to the neighborhood Bud Powell.
Yeah, you got that too.
Philly had so much diversity, between dancing schools, Judamarn (?), Johnny Hines, you know just a variety of cultures. The Academy of Music was a place you go on Saturday to see different things.
So a very, very rich cultural center.
Yeah, Philadelphia started out that way. It was the capitol of the United States for a while.
Right!
So it had a lot of history.
I wouldn’t have wanted to grow up any place else, and he’d say the same thing.
